1.pericope_label: Jethro hears, and brings Moses his wife and sons

schools.summary: Calvin dissents from the general opinion about the separation. Most commentators think Zipporah, enraged over her son's circumcision, turned back on the journey and went to live with her father; but Calvin gives three reasons against it — Moses would never have allowed his sons to be deprived of the redemption of which he was himself the minister, it would not have been consistent that they should afterwards be appointed priests of a God who was not their Redeemer, and had he deposited his family in safety and advanced alone to the contest he would have been deservedly suspected of deceit or of excessive cowardice. He applies the clause about sending her back to the wilderness rather than to Egypt, Moses having sent his wife to visit her father out of respect to an old man nearly connected with him; and he finds in the sons' names a proof of magnanimity, since Moses cannot but have brought on himself the ill-will of his connections by calling their country a strange land. Gill adds that the Targums style Jethro the prince of Midian.

Henry gives Jethro two errands and Wesley the same two after him: to congratulate the happiness of Israel and the honour of Moses, and to bring back his wife and children. Though as a Midianite Jethro was not to share in the promised land he shared in the joy of the deliverance, and we may thus make the comforts of others our own by taking pleasure, as God does, in the prosperity of the righteous. Henry defends the earlier separation, since Moses foresaw what discouragements he was likely to meet in Pharaoh's court, but insists the parting could only be temporary, husbands being commanded to dwell with their wives. He reads Gershom, a stranger, as a memorial of Moses's own condition and a memorandum to his son of his, since we are all strangers upon earth as all our fathers were; and Eliezer, my God a help, either backward to the deliverance after the slaying of the Egyptian or forward, as the original will bear, the Lord is my help and will deliver me from the sword of Pharaoh. He closes with a chronological caution, that the incident may well have happened where it stands, before the giving of the law.

Clarke states the common view that Zipporah had been alarmed at the danger to her son's life and left her husband, but allows the alternative that Moses himself sent them back, foreseeing the troubles they would meet in Egypt, and that Jethro, finding God had delivered them, thought it proper to bring them while Moses was near Horeb. He also suggests that Jethro was the son of Reuel, and so the brother-in-law rather than the father-in-law of Moses, the Hebrew word so translated meaning simply a relative by marriage. Wesley follows Henry throughout, adding only that Moses seems to have sent his family back from the inn where his wife's unwillingness to have her son circumcised had like to have cost him his life.

Ellicott follows Eliezer beyond the naming, supposing him the boy Zipporah circumcised in the wilderness, who grew to manhood and had a son Rehabiah whose descendants were very numerous in the time of David; whether Moses gave him the name before parting from him, in allusion to his escape from the Pharaoh who sought to slay him, or first on receiving him back, in allusion to the host destroyed in the sea, Ellicott leaves uncertain. Keil summarises only that Moses received his father-in-law with the honour due to his rank.

debates.question: Why were Zipporah and her sons not with Moses in Egypt?

positions.position: either Zipporah turned back of her own accord, alarmed over the circumcision at the inn, or Moses sent them back foreseeing the troubles of Egypt — Clarke allows both
neither; Moses underwent the bondage together with his household, and the sending back belongs to the wilderness

outliers.note: traces Eliezer's line to Rehabiah and his numerous descendants in the time of David, and leaves open whether the name was given at the parting or at the reunion

themes: Jethro brings back Zipporah and her two sons
whether Moses had sent his family away
the sense of the names Gershom and Eliezer

5.pericope_label: Jethro comes to the mount of God

schools.summary: Calvin asks what brought the old man out and answers that it was not so much love for Moses as the fame of the miracles which drew him, bowed down with age, from his home into the wilderness. That he was not induced by ambition appears from the sequel, since after he had offered sacrifice and in solemn thanksgiving ascribed all the glory to God alone he returned home again with the same simplicity in which he had come; and Moses himself states the cause at the head of the chapter, saying not that Jethro had heard of his son-in-law's arrival but how wonderful had been God's goodness and power in delivering the people. As to the title of the place, the vision already vouchsafed there had made Horeb worthy of the name, but the reference here is rather to the promulgation of the law, whereby God consecrated the mountain to Himself. Gill notices only that this is the third time in the chapter Jethro is called Moses's father-in-law, either to distinguish him or to do him honour.

Clarke argues at length that the visit stands out of its chronological place. Israel had not yet reached Horeb, which they did not arrive at till the third month, whereas the transactions this account is joined to fall in the second; Moses relates in Deuteronomy that it was when they were about to depart from Horeb, in the second year, that he complained he could not bear the burden of government alone and established captains over thousands and hundreds and fifties and tens, which appears to be the very transaction recorded here; Moses speaks below of the statutes and laws of the Lord as already revealed; and Jethro offers burnt-offerings in the manner the law commands, though that law was not yet given. Clarke would therefore insert the chapter in Numbers, where Moses entreats Hobab to stay as a guide, but adds that the matter is not of much importance. He offers a reason why it stands where it does: Moses had just related the war with Amalek and the curse laid upon them, and may be showing Jethro free from that curse, although the Kenites of his family dwelt among the Amalekites. On the message he agrees with Gill that Jethro was not yet present, and supports the reading behold for I on the authority of the Greek and Syriac and several Samaritan copies.

Ellicott meets the same chronological difficulty more mildly, allowing that the mount of God may here be used broadly of the entire Sinaitic mountain region, or that the movement described in the next chapter may have taken place before Jethro's arrival though not related until after it, since Exodus was probably composed in detached portions and arranged afterwards.

debates.question: Does this chapter stand in its true chronological place?

positions.position: no; it belongs in Numbers, after the erection of the tabernacle and the giving of the law
not necessarily; the mount of God may be used broadly, or the march may be related out of order, Exodus being composed in detached portions

themes: Jethro arrives at the mount of God
whether the chapter stands in its chronological place
the announcement sent ahead by messenger

7.pericope_label: Moses goes out to meet him, and tells him all

schools.summary: Gill draws a moral from the going out: one at the head of such a vast body of people condescended to go in person, when a guard of his men would have been honour sufficient; and he adds from Aben Ezra that Moses is not said to go out to meet his wife and children, since it was not usual for honourable men so to do. Calvin notes only that the previous verse related what happened last, this transposition being common in Hebrew.

Henry makes the greeting a lesson in place. Though Moses was a prophet of the Lord, a great prophet, and king in Jeshurun, he showed a very humble respect to his father-in-law: however God is pleased to advance us, we must make conscience of giving honour to whom honour is due, and never look with disdain upon our poor relations, for those that stand high in God's favour are not thereby discharged from the duty they owe to men. Religion does not destroy good manners. Conversation concerning God's wondrous works is profitable conversation, and asking and telling news is capable of being turned to good account by taking notice of God's providence. Jethro rejoiced not only in the honour done his son-in-law but in all the goodness done to Israel — public blessings are the joy of public spirits, and while the Israelites were themselves murmuring here was a Midianite rejoicing, not the only time the faith of the Gentiles shamed the unbelief of the Jews. His confession that the Lord is greater than all gods Henry takes as knowledge he had before but now held better, his faith grown to full assurance on this fresh evidence; and Jethro, hearty in Israel's interests, was cheerfully admitted though a Midianite into fellowship with Moses and the elders, forasmuch as he also was a son of Abraham, though of a younger house.

Clarke reads the three acts as good breeding and politeness accompanied with sincerity — bowing down the general token of respect, the kiss the token of friendship, the enquiry after welfare the proof of affectionate intercourse. On the tent they entered he reports that some understand the tabernacle, and that Moses may have taken his relative first to the house of God before bringing him to his own.

Ellicott sets the gestures among the customs of the country. Oriental etiquette required the going forth to meet an honoured guest, as with Abraham and Lot; the obeisance, however, was wholly voluntary, and marks the humility of Moses, who, now that he was the prince of his nation, might well have required Jethro to bow down to him. Kissing is a common form of salutation in the East, even between persons in no way related, and he quotes Herodotus on the Persians, that when they meet in the streets you may know if they are of equal rank by this token, for if they are, instead of speaking they kiss each other on the lips, while if one is a little inferior the kiss is given on the cheek. The asking after welfare he renders literally, that they wished peace to each other.

outliers.note: documents the kiss of salutation from Herodotus on the Persians, where equals kiss on the lips and a slight inferior on the cheek

themes: the kind greeting between Moses and Jethro
the narrative of what God had done
kissing and obeisance as Eastern salutation

8.pericope_label: Jethro blesses the LORD and offers sacrifice

schools.summary: Calvin weighs the confession carefully and finds it genuine but not pure. Although the worship of God was then everywhere profaned by strange additions, Jethro was not so devoted to superstition as to fail to honour the true God, and by the name Jehovah he plainly designates the God of Israel. Yet the comparison he adds, that Jehovah is greater than all gods, implies he was not free from all error: the prophets speak so with a different import, whereas Jethro imagines with the common notion that a multitude of inferior gods are subordinate to the Most High — and where the pure truth of God does not shine, religion is never clear, but always has some dregs mixed with it. Calvin allows him some advance, since in affirming that he now knows the power of God he implies he was more rightly informed than before. On the clause about dealing proudly he observes that the sentence is unfinished, the principal verb wanting to express that God repaid the Egyptians the just wages of their cruelty; the exposition that the Egyptians who drowned the infants were themselves drowned seems to him too limited, and he extends the clause to every punishment they received. On the sacrifice he holds the meal proves the offering lawful, since the elders came not merely to eat bread with Jethro but before God, and would never have polluted themselves to gratify an unholy man; but he denies Jethro slew the victims in right of his Midianite priesthood, holding rather that there was more liberty before the law was given, and says that by bread the manna is incontestably meant. Gill sees behind the idols the evil demons who influenced the magicians.

Clarke is firmer than Calvin about Jethro's standing: some think he was now converted, but he probably had this blessing before he knew anything of Moses, who would not likely have married into a heathen family. He takes the pride of the Egyptians to be their tyranny in enslaving God's people while purposing yet more, and God above them in showing himself superior to their gods by the miracles he wrought. Having Jethro a priest by right, he takes the burnt offering as presumptive evidence that the tabernacle was already erected, since before God means before the place where God dwelt. Wesley reads the confession of princes as well as gods, and notes only that they ate soberly and thankfully, their talk such as became saints.

Ellicott narrows the clause about dealing proudly to the matter in which the Egyptians dealt most proudly — pursuing Israel with an army after giving them leave to depart, and attempting to recapture or destroy them. On the sacrifice he says Jethro had brought the victims with him and now offered them in thankfulness for God's mercies to himself and his kinsman, occupying a position like Melchizedek's, a priesthood of the most primitive character, probably as patriarch of his tribe; and as Abraham rightly acknowledged Melchizedek's priesthood, so Moses and Aaron acknowledged Jethro's, indicating their acceptance of it by sharing the sacrificial meal which followed.

debates.question: What is meant by the clause, wherein they dealt proudly, he was above them?

positions.position: every instance of punishment the Egyptians received, not merely a drowning for a drowning
specifically the pursuit with an army after Israel had been given leave to depart
their tyranny in enslaving God’s people while purposing yet more

positions.position: by a primitive priesthood like Melchizedek’s, held as patriarch of his tribe
not by his Midianite priesthood, but by the greater liberty that obtained before the law was given

13.pericope_label: Moses sits to judge the people from morning to evening

schools.summary: Calvin thinks the passage memorable because the fault is found in so good a man. In a government over which God presided, and which He honoured with extraordinary manifestations of His glory, there was something deserving reprehension, and Moses, with whom alone God was thus familiar, was deservedly reproved for wearing away both himself and the people by excessive labour. It was a magnanimity never sufficiently praised that he should occupy himself gratuitously for this perverse people though assailed by reproaches; yet Jethro finds occasion of fault in these very praises. Whence we are warned that in the most excellent acts of men some defect is ever lurking: let all, whether kings or magistrates or pastors, know that while they strain every nerve to fulfil their duties, something will always remain which may admit of correction. No single mortal can be sufficient to do everything — for who shall equal Moses, and he was unequal to the burden. As one ray of the sun does not illuminate the world but all combine as one, so God, that He may retain men in mutual society, unites one to another by variously dispensing His gifts, and raises up none out of measure by entire perfection; and Calvin ends with Augustine, that God humbled His servant by this act, as Paul was buffeted lest his revelations exalt him. Gill notes the Targum's dating of the morrow to the day after the atonement, preferring the day after Jethro came.

Henry reads the day as a display of zeal. Having been employed to redeem Israel out of bondage, Moses is here a further type of Christ in being lawgiver and judge among them: his business was not to make laws but to make known God's, his place being that of a servant. Henry marks four things that might have excused him and did not — his father-in-law's presence, pretext enough for a vacation, though necessary business must take place of ceremonious attentions; his advancement to great honour, which did not tempt him to throw the burden of care upon others, since those think of themselves above what is meet who think it below them to do good; the people's readiness to stone him, though he still made himself the servant of all; and his age, though he kept to it from morning to night, proof that after all his labours his natural force was not diminished.

Clarke says only that Moses heard and determined controversies, obliged to sit all day while the people were continually coming and going; Wesley, that he sat to answer enquiries and explain the laws already given.

Ellicott sets the scene in the institutions of the age. The office of prince or ruler was in early times regarded as including that of judge; rulers were sometimes even called judges, as were those of Israel from Joshua to Samuel, and ability to judge marked a person out as fit for the kingly office. Moses had from the first undertaken the hearing of all complaints, holding court days when the host was stationary, and no cause was decided by anyone else — either because it had not occurred to him to discharge the duty by deputy, or because he thought his countrymen unfit. That the people stood by him all day shows the causes either very many or very hard, and some have suggested that the division of the Amalekite spoil would have led to disputes. Keil adds that the people came to seek God, that is, to ask a decision from Him, and that by deciding the cases Moses made known the ordinances and laws of God, for every decision rested on some law, which, like all true justice, emanated first from God.

outliers.note: turns the episode into a warning against taking on too much, since God dispenses gifts variously and raises up none out of measure by entire perfection

themes: Moses sits alone to judge from morning to evening
the fault that lurks in the most excellent acts
judging as the ancient office of the ruler

14.pericope_label: Jethro objects: the thing that thou doest is not good

schools.summary: Calvin gathers a doctrine of magistracy out of Moses's answer. Moses replies ingenuously, like one unconscious of any fault, declaring himself the minister of God and the organ of His Spirit; his faithfulness could not be called in question, for he erred only in overwhelming himself with labour. Yet since he says that disputants come to inquire of God, and that he makes them know the statutes of God and His laws, it follows that this is the object of political government, that God's tribunal should be erected on earth, wherein He may exercise the judge's office — to the end that magistrates should not arrogate a power uncontrolled by any laws, nor assume what belongs to God. Then, and then only, will they acquit themselves properly: when they remember that they are the representatives of God. An obligation lies on private individuals too, that they should not rashly appeal to the authority of judges but approach them with pure hearts, as if inquiring of God. On the reproof itself Calvin admires Jethro's moderation: he does not condemn the whole system, after the fashion of morose or ambitious men who by carping at some trifle obscure the noble deeds of others, but by correcting only a part detracts nothing from the just praise of Moses. Gill, following Aben Ezra, distinguishes the two things Moses did — teaching them the mind of God, and deciding causes — and hears in the warning about wearing away an allusion to the leaves of trees in autumn, which fade and wither and fall.

Clarke explains the first of Moses's offices as mediation, since the people came to him to know what God had spoken, and finds in the phrasing about the statutes another argument for his chronology, the words being so particular that they leave little room for doubt the law had already been given. On the warning he renders the doubled Hebrew verb as in wearing away thou wilt wear away, so that Moses would soon become finally exhausted, and the people with him, since many wait so long that their patience must necessarily be worn out. Wesley remarks of the second office that if the people were as quarrelsome with one another as with God, Moses had many causes before him, the more because their trials put them to no expense; and he compresses Jethro's verdict to a phrase — not good, that is, not convenient either for him or for them.

Ellicott says the emphatic word in Jethro's question is alone, and states Moses's two arguments more fully than Moses does: the people want decisions which they can feel to have divine sanction, and the ruling of inferior judges would not be regarded as equally authoritative; and Moses does not simply decide the question brought before him, but takes the opportunity to instruct the people in delivering his judgments, expounding principles and teaching morality. Both reasons were clearly of great weight, yet they failed to convince Jethro, who answered that Moses would exhaust both his own strength and the patience of the people, since to keep suitors waiting all day and perhaps dismiss them untried was not fair upon them.

outliers.note: reconstructs the two arguments for Moses's practice — that the people wanted decisions felt to carry divine sanction, and that he taught while he judged

themes: why sittest thou thyself alone
the magistrate as the representative of God
thou wilt surely wear away

19.pericope_label: Jethro's counsel: able men as rulers of thousands

schools.summary: Calvin insists that Jethro does not rob Moses of his authority so as to overturn his call from God, but by exhorting him to proceed desires that what God has ordained should remain inviolable. On the choice of judges he says the word rendered provide means to choose out and take the most worthy, so that such an office be not entrusted rashly to any that offers; and among a free people judges should be chosen not for wealth or rank but for superiority in virtue. Jethro enumerates four qualifications — ability in business, the fear of God, integrity, and contempt of riches — not to exclude the others named in Deuteronomy, but to signify that extraordinary virtues are wanted. The Hebrew men of might some take for strong and laborious men capable of bearing fatigue, but in Calvin's opinion Moses designates rather strenuous and courageous persons, opposed to the timid as well as the inactive; piety comes second because vigour of mind and body alike is frail without the fear of God; truth is opposed not only to gross falsehood but to popularity-hunting and flattery; and hatred of covetousness is demanded because nothing is more antagonistic to justice than eagerness for gain. He reads the arrangement as provisional, Jethro having no wish to establish a law for posterity but pointing out a remedy until the people should obtain a peaceful resting-place, and takes the clause about God commanding as a self-correction, since Jethro would have nothing conceded to him which derogates from God's authority. Gill observes that Jethro, as the elder man and a prince of Midian, might counsel a younger man without censure.

Clarke thinks Jethro a man of great understanding whose advice was probably given under the immediate inspiration of God, since after such sacrificial rites the prophetic spirit might well be expected to rest upon him; God could have shown Moses the necessity directly, but chose in this case to help man by man, and so laid a permanent basis for the union of the two families. He traces the ladder of appeal upward past Moses to God, and reports that some rabbins reckoned seventy-eight thousand six hundred officers in all — such computations, he says, are fanciful, since we cannot tell how many of each division there were. Wesley puts the qualifications more briskly: clear heads and stout hearts make good judges.

Ellicott renders the clause about God's presence as a wish — may God be with thee, may He give thee wisdom to direct the course aright — and reads the charge as an instruction to remain representative of the people towards God and of God towards the people, taking difficult causes to Him and expounding His laws. He finds the organisation unsurprising: in Egypt, as in all settled governments, the king was the fountain of justice but delegated the hearing of causes to officials of different ranks, and in Arabia a similar practice prevailed, Jethro himself having subordinates who judged small matters. His advice was simply that Moses adopt this established system, on a decimal organisation which may already have existed for the march and the encamping, with appeal from the ruler of ten upward to the ruler of a thousand. The judges were to sit not on occasional court days but continually, and it must have been left to them to decide what were great and what small matters; when the wilderness life ended, Jethro's system ended with it. Of the qualifications Ellicott notes that the last two would approve themselves to men of all times and countries, while the first would generally be deemed superfluous, though it lies at the root of all excellence of character.

outliers.note: dismisses as fanciful the rabbinic and Josephan computations of the number of officers, since the divisions are known but not their multiples

themes: be thou for the people to God-ward
the qualifications of a judge
rulers of thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens

24.pericope_label: Moses takes the counsel, and Jethro departs

schools.summary: Calvin finds the submission remarkable. Here is an instance of modesty, that Moses is not indisposed to submit to the counsel of his father-in-law; for although Jethro was his superior in age and affinity, in other respects he was far inferior to him. This yielding lays down a rule for all the greatest doctors, that they should not refuse the admonitions of those whom they admit to teach rightly, although they are not of such high dignity — for Cyprian truly declares that none is a good doctor who is not also docile. Gill says Moses weighed the advice well and judged it good, resolving to follow it when he had received directions from God; he notices that though only the first of Jethro's qualifications is named in the record of the choice, no doubt all were attended to, and that the new judges sat any day in the week and any time in the day. He reports the Targum's note that Jethro went to proselytise the children of his own country.

Clarke turns the departure into a meditation on Moses himself. If this be the same transaction related in Numbers, it was with great reluctance that Moses let so able a counsellor go, pressing him to stay and be instead of eyes to them in the desert; but Jethro chose rather to return to his own country, where his family were probably too settled to be removed — many others might be eyes to the Hebrews in the desert, but no man could be a father to his family but himself, and though it is well to labour for the public good, our own families are the first claimants on our care and time. It is strange, he adds, that after this we hear no more of Zipporah, forgotten merely because she was the wife of Moses, who chose to conduct himself so that to the remotest ages there should be proofs of his disinterestedness: while multitudes of the families of Israel are celebrated and dignified, his own he writes in the dust, and he made no provision even for Gershom and Eliezer, whose families were incorporated with the Levites. No history, Clarke concludes, has produced a parallel to this disinterestedness, and the one consideration is sufficient to refute every charge of imposture brought against him and his laws. Wesley draws the moral of the submission: those are not so wise as they would be thought to be who think themselves too wise to be counselled, for a wise man will hear and will increase learning, and not slight good counsel though given by an inferior; and he notes that the Kenites are supposed to be Jethro's posterity, taken afterwards under special protection for the kindness their ancestor showed Israel.

Keil looks at the shape of the arrangement. The judges chosen were made chiefs over thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens, after the analogy of the military organisation on the march, but so that the arrangement was linked to the natural division of the people into tribes and families. That the decimal division was not made arbitrarily according to the number of heads is evident on two grounds: the judges were chosen from the heads of the tribes and according to their tribes; and the larger divisions of the tribes, the families, were themselves called thousands, because the number of their heads of families would generally average about a thousand — so that in all probability the hundreds and fifties and tens denote smaller natural divisions rather than counted groups. Ellicott takes the dismissal as evidence against a common identification: the supposed identity of Hobab with Jethro seems precluded by it, for Hobab clearly remained till the close of the stay at Sinai, and Moses, instead of dismissing him, was most unwilling that he should depart.

debates.question: Is Hobab the same person as Jethro?

positions.position: no; Moses dismissed Jethro here, whereas he was most unwilling that Hobab should depart, and Hobab remained till the close of the stay at Sinai
the two accounts are of one transaction, in which Moses pressed his father-in-law to stay and be instead of eyes to them

themes: Moses hearkens to the voice of his father-in-law
the decimal organisation and the tribes
